g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Charts are ubiquitous in scientific publications, business reports, and data journalism, serving as a primary medium for communicating quantitative information.

g.text: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made substantial progress on chart

g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=2) Vision-language models (VLMs) have made substantial progress on chart question answering, with recent benchmarks such as ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) and ChartQAPro (Masry et al., 2025) driving advances in visual reasoning over data visualizations.

g.text: However, these benchmarks predominantly evaluate performance on clean,

g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) However, these benchmarks predominantly evaluate performance on clean, high-quality images, leaving a critical gap in understanding how VLMs perform under realistic deployment conditions.

g.text: Real-world chart images are frequently degraded by compression artifacts,
blur from scanning or screenshots, pixelation from low-resolution sources,
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) Real-world chart images are frequently degraded by compression artifacts, blur from scanning or screenshots, pixelation from low-resolution sources, and noise from photocopying.

g.text: Recent studies have shown that VLMs suffer dramatic performance drops under
such corruptions (Shin et al., 2025; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2024), with
accuracy declining by 25–30 percentage points on blurred or pixelated
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=2) Recent studies have shown that VLMs suffer dramatic performance drops under such corruptions (Shin et al., 2025; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2024), with accuracy declining by 25–30 percentage points on blurred or pixelated charts.

g.text: The primary failure mode is text illegibility: when axis labels, tick marks,
legend entries, and titles become unreadable, VLMs cannot extract the
information needed to answer questions, even when their visual reasoning
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) The primary failure mode is text illegibility: when axis labels, tick marks, legend entries, and titles become unreadable, VLMs cannot extract the information needed to answer questions, even when their visual reasoning capabilities remain intact.

g.text: Existing approaches to improving robustness typically require retraining
models on augmented data or developing specialized architectures (Masry et
al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), which is expensive and may not generalize to
g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Existing approaches to improving robustness typically require retraining models on augmented data or developing specialized architectures (Masry et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), which is expensive and may not generalize to new corruption types.

g.text: OCR recovers text better than VLMs
We observe that OCR systems, which are specifically optimized for text
extraction, can often recover text from degraded images more reliably than
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) We observe that OCR systems, which are specifically optimized for text extraction, can often recover text from degraded images more reliably than VLM vision encoders.

g.text: Q: OCR text at inference time?

providing OCR-extracted text to VLMs at inference time, without any model
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) This motivates a simple question: can we improve chart QA robustness by providing OCR-extracted text to VLMs at inference time, without any model modification?

g.text: We propose ReInk, a training-free inference wrapper that extracts text from
corrupted charts using OCR and renders it as a spatially-aligned auxiliary
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) We propose ReInk, a training-free inference wrapper that extracts text from corrupted charts using OCR and renders it as a spatially-aligned auxiliary image.

g.text: By providing both the corrupted chart and the re-inked canvas to the VLM, we
give the model access to legible text while preserving the original chart's
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) By providing both the corrupted chart and the re-inked canvas to the VLM, we give the model access to legible text while preserving the original chart's visual structure.

g.text: Our experiments on ChartQAPro-Corrupted demonstrate that ReInk improves

g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) Our experiments on ChartQAPro-Corrupted demonstrate that ReInk improves accuracy by +12.21 percentage points (27.95% vs 15.74% baseline), with gains scaling predictably with OCR quality.

g.text: We propose ReInk, a training-free inference wrapper that improves
VLM robustness on corrupted charts by providing OCR-extracted text
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose ReInk, a training-free inference wrapper that improves VLM robustness on corrupted charts by providing OCR-extracted text as a spatially-rendered auxiliary image.

g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We conduct comprehensive experiments on ChartQAPro-Corrupted, demonstrating +12.21pp improvement over baseline and +8.50pp over a scrambled-text control, confirming that correct text semantics drive the gains.

g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We analyze what components matter: text content is the primary driver (+11.57pp from OCR text alone), while spatial rendering (+0.64pp) and bounding box outlines (+0.10pp) provide marginal additional benefit.
